body.heading: Measuring the whole sky
paragraphs: A forecast begins as a census of the atmosphere. Weather stations, ships, aircraft, ocean buoys and weather balloons report temperature, pressure, wind and humidity, while satellites and radar watch from above. Twice a day, hundreds of balloons rise simultaneously around the world, sampling the air up to the edge of the stratosphere.
All of this pours into a few forecasting centres, where the first task is simply to agree on what the atmosphere looks like right now — a three-dimensional snapshot of a restless ocean of air.

body.heading: A planet inside a computer
paragraphs: Supercomputers divide the atmosphere into millions of boxes and apply the laws of physics to each one: air flows, rises, cools, forms clouds. Then they step the whole virtual planet forward minutes at a time, computing days of weather in hours of calculation.

Because tiny errors grow — the famous butterfly effect — forecasters run the model many times with slightly different starting points. If most runs agree on rain, confidence is high; if they scatter, the forecast honestly becomes a probability.

body.heading: Better than you remember
paragraphs: Forecasts have improved steadily, roughly gaining a day of skill per decade: today's four-day forecast is about as accurate as the one-day forecast of the 1990s. Storm warnings now save lives that would once have been lost without notice.
Yet the atmosphere keeps its secrets past about two weeks, where chaos wins. The forecast is not a promise — it is physics, statistics and humility, delivered with your morning news.

takeaway: Forecasts come from measuring the whole atmosphere and simulating it many times over — skill that improves yearly, bounded by honest chaos.
